solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Location of cash register, matter for investigation

parts.note: to note = to register, take notice of
a case is what a detective or court investigates

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper's till has become the subject of a police inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cash register' reads as one thing, the till; the definition stops at 'cash' and 'register' is a verb starting the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A notecase is an old word for a wallet, the place banknotes are kept.

clue.text: Only virtue it seems for tenderfoot

parts.note: someone with only virtue has no ...
... vice, a flaw; 'it seems' flags a playful reading of the letters as two words

explanation.surface: A remark that beginners seem to be nothing but virtuous.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a description, not a list of parts: having only virtue means having no vice, and NO VICE run together is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenderfoot is a newcomer or beginner, exactly what a novice is.

clue.text: One body part, not another according to Spooner

indicators.note: Rev William Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so his version of a phrase swaps its initial sounds

parts.note: 'not another' body part = NO TAIL; NO takes the T of TAIL
TAIL takes the N of NO

explanation.surface: One part of the body is named, and another is said to be missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' means another body part, a tail: being without one is 'no tail', and Spooner turns that into toenail.
explanation.definitionFit: A toenail is a part of the body, the hard plate on the end of a toe.

clue.text: Chelsea bun cooked for a couple of supporters?

indicators.note: cooking changes the form of the ingredients, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A baker's Chelsea bun is baked for two fans of the London football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' pretends to mean football fans, and Chelsea helps the lie; it means the two heels a shoe-wearer stands on. A Chelsea bun is a spiral currant bun.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuban heels are a pair of medium, slightly tapered shoe heels, and heels hold the wearer up, hence supporters.

clue.text: Rul-ing by the majority?

parts.note: a ruling, printed with a hyphen that splits it in two
a verdict carried by most of the judges, with the rest dissenting

explanation.surface: A judgement handed down by most, but not all, of a panel.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray hyphen is the joke: the word 'ruling' is itself split, and a ruling is a decision.
explanation.definitionFit: A split decision is one where the judges disagree and the majority carries it, as in boxing.

clue.text: Poem I penned in month, as divine

indicators.note: something penned in is shut inside an enclosure

parts.note: DEC = December, the calendar abbreviation
'If' is Kipling's famous poem
I as written

explanation.surface: A poet claims godlike powers for a verse written during one month.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's 'If', beginning 'If you can keep your head', is the crossword's favourite poem, so 'poem' is worth reading as those two letters first.
explanation.definitionFit: Deific means making divine or godlike, so it can stand for divine.

clue.text: Love for Grecians, love for no Romans, ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so take the last letter of each word

parts.note: last letters of lovE foR nO romanS

explanation.surface: The Greeks had love, the Romans in the end had none.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue repeats 'love for' so the second half looks like a parallel definition; it is the fodder whose word endings spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek word, and god, for erotic love.

clue.text: Crafty beer for player

parts.note: fly = sharp, knowing, crafty (British slang)
a half = half a pint of beer, a British pub order

explanation.surface: Craft beer handed to a sportsman after the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crafty beer' suggests craft beer; it is two words doing separate jobs. A fly-half is the rugby back who directs play.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the position names the rugby back who wears the number ten shirt and directs attacks.

clue.text: Wedge, say, taking divot before a possible splash?

parts.note: a wedge is a kind of golf club
a divot is a piece of turf, a sod
A as written

explanation.surface: A golfer takes a divot with a wedge before the ball lands in water.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf picture makes 'splash' a water hazard; in a bar a splash is a little soda added to a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Club soda is soda water, and a splash of it is what goes into a whisky.

clue.text: Fight scene cut

indicators.note: cutting a word takes a piece off its end

parts.note: a view = a scene

explanation.surface: A brawl is edited out of a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scene cut' sounds like film editing; the scene is a view, and cutting its tail leaves VIE.
explanation.definitionFit: To vie is to compete or contend, to fight for something.

clue.text: Solver's beef well done!

parts.note: bully beef is tinned corned beef
the solver is 'you', and what is the solver's is for you

explanation.surface: Someone is congratulated on a steak cooked all the way through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well done' pretends to be how the beef is cooked; it is the exclamation, the definition. Bully beef is the corned beef of army rations.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Bully for you!' is a congratulation, often sarcastic, meaning well done.

clue.text: Settle resolution that may help Polish

definitions.meaning: Settle is a town in Yorkshire, and resolution is grit, so the determination of its people
a fine abrasive stone from the county, rubbed on metal and stone to polish them

explanation.surface: A plea for help settling a resolution with Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: Both capitals mislead: Settle is a North Yorkshire market town, not a verb, and Polish is the verb, not the nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkshire grit is both the proverbial stubbornness of Yorkshire folk and a polishing stone.

clue.text: Establishment opening on concourse to which another is possibly linked?

definitions.text: Establishment opening on concourse to which another is possibly linked?

parts.note: a shop opening in a station or mall concourse

parts.words: to which another is possibly linked?
parts.note: a chain has linked branches, one shop joined to others of the same name

explanation.surface: A new shop in a station hall, with another branch connected to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linked' is the pun: branches of a chain are metaphorically links of one chain.
explanation.definitionFit: A chain store is one of many shops under the same ownership, linked like a chain.

clue.text: World is hurting

definitions.meaning: a world in the planetary sense: the red planet, fourth from the sun
a verb in the third person: spoils, damages

explanation.surface: A lament that the whole world is in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'World' reads as the Earth we live on; here it is another world, a planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars is a planet, a world; it also mars, or harms, something.

clue.text: Prophet for instance in dummy

indicators.note: one thing in another goes inside it

parts.note: a dummy is a British baby's pacifier, also called a soother
say = for instance

explanation.surface: A prophet appears as an example inside a ventriloquist's dummy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dummy' suggests a mannequin or fool; in Britain it is a baby's pacifier, also called a soother.
explanation.definitionFit: A soothsayer foretells the future, which is what a prophet does.

clue.text: Bolero's piece for record cover?

definitions.meaning: a bolero is a short open jacket; the piece is one of its arms
the card packet a vinyl LP is stored in

explanation.surface: A request for a recording of Ravel's Bolero to go on an album cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Bolero pretends to be Ravel's orchestral piece, which is exactly the thing a record holds; it is the short jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeve is an arm of a garment and the card cover of a record.

clue.text: Derided and put away rapidly

definitions.meaning: to scoff food is to eat it greedily, in British slang

explanation.surface: Someone was mocked and then quickly locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' suggests jailing someone; it is eating, as in putting away a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoffed means both jeered and wolfed down.

clue.text: Cupboard containing empty space with little room in between

indicators.note: containing means holding something inside

parts.note: a closet is a cupboard

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its insides, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: SpacE with its middle removed

explanation.surface: A cupboard with a gap in it and barely any room around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' is a common signal: the word keeps only its first and last letters. The insertion point is not at the middle, so try each gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Close-set means placed near together, as eyes can be, with little room between.

clue.text: Knowledge and gift of flowers entrancing woman

parts.note: lore = traditional knowledge
a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers, given as a welcome

explanation.surface: A woman is won over by learning and a bunch of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrancing' reads as part of the courtship; it describes the woman, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei is the Rhine siren who lured boatmen; the name now means any alluring woman.

clue.text: Thief who's guilty of disturbing the peace?

definitions.text: Thief who's guilty of disturbing the peace?

parts.note: reads as any burglar; the thief in mind steals cattle or horses

parts.words: who's guilty of disturbing the peace?
parts.note: reads as a public-order offence; taken literally, it is someone who breaks the quiet with a soft crackling noise

explanation.surface: A burglar also charged with breach of the peace.
explanation.walkthrough: Disturbing the peace is a legal charge, which fits a thief; here the disturbance is just the rustling noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustler is a livestock thief, and one who rustles breaks the quiet.

clue.text: Friend's struck out at eventually

indicators.note: something struck out is crossed out of the text

parts.note: an intimate is a close friend
remove AT

explanation.surface: A friend eventually lashed out at someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struck out at' reads as lashing out; it is the instruction to delete the letters AT from INTIMATE. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean after enough of a wait, sooner or later.

clue.text: Con essentially cleaned out Rembrandt, stitching up great artist

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reverses the letters
the essence of a word is its centre

parts.note: the middle letter of cOn

indicators.note: a word cleaned out has its insides removed, leaving the outer letters

parts.note: RembrandT with its insides gone
a seam is a line of stitching

explanation.surface: A conman strips a Rembrandt bare, framing an old master.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stitching up' sounds like framing someone for the con; SEAM is the stitching, and 'up' turns ORTSEAM over.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a master, especially of music, so a great artist.

clue.text: Flip coin finally into fountain, to return

indicators.note: finally means the last letter
one thing going into another sits inside it

parts.note: the Trevi Fountain in Rome, where tourists throw coins

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: last letter of coiN

explanation.surface: Toss a coin into the Trevi Fountain so you return to Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the tradition: throwing a coin into the Trevi Fountain means you will return to Rome. N goes into IVERT, the fountain reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: To invert is to turn upside down, to flip.

clue.text: Unexceptional rascal, and playing truant

indicators.note: a truant is absent, so AND goes missing from the word

parts.note: a so-and-so is a rascal
remove AND

explanation.surface: An ordinary scamp who skips school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like a link word between two clue parts; it is the letters deleted from SO-AND-SO. Playing truant is skipping school.
explanation.definitionFit: So-so means middling, neither good nor bad.

clue.text: Film maker with great intellect screening coverage of Sartre?

indicators.note: a screen hides something behind or within it

parts.note: Albert Einstein, byword for genius

indicators.note: the covering of a word is its outer letters

parts.note: the outside letters of SartrE

explanation.surface: A brainy film director shows a documentary about Sartre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screening' and 'film maker' make a cinema picture; screening means holding within. Sergei Eisenstein made Battleship Potemkin.
explanation.definitionFit: Eisenstein was a pioneering Soviet film director.

clue.text: Bird in garden, redbreast soaring

indicators.note: the answer is inside the words that follow
in a down clue, soaring means rising, so the letters read upward

parts.note: inside gardEN REdbreast

explanation.surface: A robin in the garden takes to the air.
explanation.walkthrough: The redbreast, a robin, is the bird the surface shows; the answer is a different bird, a sea eagle.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle.

clue.text: Lo! "Green" rays converted?

indicators.note: converting changes something into another form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: Behold: sunlight turned into clean, environmentally friendly power.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: solar energy is green power made by converting the sun's rays.
explanation.definitionFit: Solar energy is renewable 'green' power converted from sunlight.

clue.text: Briefly rank equal in competition

indicators.note: a brief word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a rank or level, as of seats in a stadium

explanation.surface: Competitors briefly share the same ranking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank equal' reads as a single phrase; the definition starts at 'equal'.
explanation.definitionFit: To tie is to finish level with a rival in a competition.

clue.text: Bird that wouldn't fly?

parts.note: reads as a flightless bird, and the heavy farmyard one fits
an idea or show that 'won't fly' fails; a total flop has a bird's name in theatre slang

explanation.surface: A question about a flightless bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wouldn't fly' means both could not take off and did not succeed; a turkey is a theatrical or film flop.
explanation.definitionFit: A turkey is both the farmyard bird and a total failure.

clue.text: Famous solicitor set off

parts.note: star = famous, as in a star player
a tout solicits custom, e.g. a ticket tout

explanation.surface: A well-known lawyer begins a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitor' suggests the British lawyer; it is someone who solicits, a tout.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both phrasal verbs mean to begin a journey.
